title: Where Am I

post.author: u/callout_desk_seonaid
post.title: I run the night call-out desk for a hill rescue team. Our app said the nearest volunteer to a lost walker was 7.8 km away. The live map put him 400 m from her, and his phone never rang.

blocks.text: The Corrieburn Hill Rescue Team is sixty volunteers spread from Killin down to Callander and across to Doune. Our app keeps each volunteer's last phone position and an available flag they switch on when they can turn out. When a call comes in, it pages the available volunteers whose position shares the caller's 4-character geohash. The developer said that's a box about 20 km across, and nobody had ever been missed.

At 23:10 on Saturday, Catriona Glendinning phoned from the south-east ridge of Ben Ledi, above Callander. Fog, a dead head torch, no path. She read her coordinates off her phone: 56.2512 N, 4.2885 W. The app paged three.

23:10:04  call   56.2512 N 4.2885 W   geohash gfhbn2   search gfhb
23:10:04  page   Fingal Lumsden    Strathyre      7.8 km
23:10:04  page   Mairi Pitcairn   Balquhidder   12.7 km
23:10:04  page   Sorley Fyfe      Lochearnhead  15.2 km
23:10:04  nearest volunteer 7.8 km   paged 3   available tonight 27

Fingal drove round and started up from the car park. I kept her talking. All night she said she could see a torch below her, beyond an old dry-stone wall that crosses the ridge. It never moved. It never came.

At 01:30 I opened the live map to see how far Fingal had got. Her dot sat on the ridge. Almost on top of it was another: Torcuil Rintoul, available since dusk, in the hut just below the wall. His phone had never rung.
The log says the nearest volunteer was 7.8 km away. The map says 400 m.

Torcuil says that near midnight he saw a light up on the ridge and took it for a farmer out after sheep. He sat with his torch at the window and waited for the phone. Fingal's party found Catriona at 04:50, cold but alive, a few hundred metres above the hut. The wall is the old parish boundary. The developer swears the app knows nothing about parishes.

Thirteen more volunteers were available that night in Kilmahog, Callander and Brig o' Turk, between 2.6 and 5.9 km from her. None of their phones rang either. What should we change before the next call?

blocks.label: live_map_0130.png

diagram.aria: The live map at 01:30, redrawn. North of 56.25 N, in cell gfhb, which the app searched: Catriona on the ridge at geohash gfhbn2, and Fingal Lumsden in Strathyre, paged, 7.8 km from her. South of 56.25 N, not searched: Torcuil Rintoul in the hut, available, not paged, 400 m from her; and 13 more available volunteers in Kilmahog, Callander and Brig o' Turk, 2.6 to 5.9 km away, not paged. The cell line and the old wall cross the ridge together.

Torcuil, in the hut 400 m from Catriona, and 13 more available volunteers between 2.6 and 5.9 km away were all south of the line.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your app files every phone under a geohash: a short code for a place, made by halving the map again and again and noting which half the point fell in. Points whose codes start with the same characters, the same prefix, sit in one box called a cell, and a longer prefix is a smaller cell. The cell line is the edge between two cells. Now the evidence. What is Torcuil's geohash, and from which character does it stop matching Catriona's? How far is her cell's far corner from her? And when the log says 'nearest volunteer', nearest out of whom?

replies.author: u/callout_desk_seonaid
replies.text: The developer looked it up. The hut is gcuzyr; Catriona was gfhbn2. They part at the second character. He says 56.25 N is a line where the second character changes, and that a 4-character cell up here is about 21.7 km wide and 19.5 km tall. Hers runs north past Lochearnhead. The search never looked south of 56.25 at all. Nearest, he admits, means nearest of the three in her cell.

comments.author: u/bigger_net_lennox
comments.text: Four characters is just too tight for hills. Every character you drop makes each cell 32 times bigger, so go to three and the box is wide enough that nobody near her falls outside it. A bigger net catches everyone. Tight cells are for pizza deliveries in a city; in rescue you want reach, and you sort the rest out on the radio.

comments.author: u/ring_them_all_gillies
comments.text: Why search at all? Page the whole team on every call. Sixty phones ring, the nearest is always among them, and whoever's closest answers first. People sign up for this knowing they'll be woken.

reply.prompt: The next call could come tonight. What should the Corrieburn team change in the app? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Use a longer prefix, 5 or 6 characters, so each cell is small and the app knows exactly where everyone is.
options.part2: The developer set the prefix to 5 characters and replayed Saturday's call. Catriona's cell became gfhbn, 2.7 km wide and 4.9 km tall, and not one available volunteer was in it. Nobody was paged at all. At 6 characters her cell, gfhbn2, is 680 by 610 m, and still empty. Torcuil's hut, 400 m away, sits in gcuzyr, across the same line at 56.25 N, which no prefix length moves. The developer stared at the empty result for a long time. Then he set it back to 4, which at least paged someone.
options.senior: A longer prefix gives a smaller cell, and a smaller cell makes it likelier that the nearest person is outside it. A matching prefix only says two points share a box; it never says they are close. Choose the length from the distance you need to search, and always look past the box's edges.

options.text: Use a shorter prefix, 3 characters: each cell is 32 times bigger, a net wide enough to catch everyone.
options.verdict: A bigger net, the same hole
options.part2: The developer set the prefix to 3 characters and replayed Saturday's call. Catriona's cell became gfh, 86.9 km wide and 156.4 km tall, from 56.25 N north to 57.66 N. Six phones rang, in no particular order: Fingal, Mairi, Sorley, two in Killin and one in Crianlarich. The nearest paged was still Fingal, 7.8 km away, and the 14 available volunteers nearer than him still weren't paged. The bottom of the bigger cell is the same line at 56.25 N. Torcuil's hut is gcuzyr and Catriona gfhbn2: they share only the first character, g, a cell about 5,000 km across.
options.senior: A bigger cell pages more people but keeps its edges, and it hands you a list with no order. A line at a coarse level splits the codes at every length below it: here 56.25 N splits them from the second character, so only a one-character cell holds both Catriona and Torcuil. Shrinking or growing the box never fixes a search that stops at the box.

options.text: Page the whole team on every call, available or not, so the nearest volunteer is always among them.
options.part2: The developer switched the search off. On the replay, all 60 phones rang, Torcuil's among them at 400 m, and so did 33 phones whose owners had marked themselves unavailable. For two weeks every call rang everyone. Then the replies slowed. People on night shifts muted the app; a father of twins turned it off. On the next real call at 02:40, eleven people answered, and nobody could tell from the app which of them was nearest, so the desk spent nine minutes on the radio sorting it out.
options.senior: Paging everyone guarantees the nearest is paged, and throws away both the available flag and any idea of who is closest. People learn to ignore a phone that rings for every call, which is a real cost in any paging system. It's a fair fallback when the search finds nobody, not a design.

options.text: Search her cell and the eight cells around it, rank everyone found by real distance, page the nearest 3.
options.part2: The developer changed the search to Catriona's cell, gfhb, and the eight cells around it: gcux, gcuz, gcvp, gfh8, gfj0, gfh9, gfhc and gfj1. Replayed, it found 27 available volunteers, worked out each one's real distance from her, and paged the nearest 3: Torcuil Rintoul at 400 m, the Kilmahog volunteer at 2.6 km and one in Callander at 3.4 km. Three phones rang, not sixty. He kept 4 characters, because the nine cells then reach at least 19.5 km from her in every direction. On Tuesday night Torcuil walked up to the wall at 23:10 with his torch and looked up the ridge. He says nobody was there, and that he waited anyway.
options.senior: Treat the geohash as a coarse filter, never the answer. Fetch her cell and the 8 around it, so nobody within one cell's smaller side of her can be missed, then compute the real distance to everyone found, sort, and page the nearest few. Choose the length from the search radius. Where nine cells hold too many people, as in a town, smaller cells, such as a quadtree's, keep the list short.

sim.title: Replay the 23:10 call on Ben Ledi
sim.lede: You're the developer, replaying Saturday's call from Catriona at 56.2512 N, 4.2885 W. The map holds the team's 60 volunteers at their last phone positions; 27 have the available flag on. The app works out a geohash for every position and for hers, and pages the available volunteers whose code starts with the same prefix as hers. Set the prefix length (3 to 6 characters), choose whether to also search the 8 cells around hers, and whether to rank: ranking works out each volunteer's real distance from her with the haversine formula (the distance along the surface of a sphere, here of radius 6371 km) and pages only the nearest 3. Or page the whole team, available or not. The stats show how many phones ring, the nearest available volunteer paged, the nearest available on the map, and how many available volunteers nearer than the one paged were missed. The close-up shows the ridge, the old wall and the cell line. The quadtree controls build a quadtree over the 60 positions and can draw it on the map: a box that splits into four quarters whenever it holds more phones than the leaf capacity you set, so crowded places get small boxes and empty hills big ones. Try a reply picks the settings for each of the four replies.
sim.tryThis: Try this: as it ran, 3 phones ring and the nearest paged is 7.8 km while the map's nearest is 400 m, with 14 available volunteers nearer than Fingal missed. Set the prefix to 5: nobody is found; at 6, still nobody. Set it to 3: 6 phones ring, nearest still 7.8 km. Page the whole team: 60 ring. Back at 4, turn on the 8 cells around hers: 27 found and 27 ring. Turn on ranking: 3 ring, nearest 400 m. Now turn the 8 cells off: ranking alone pages Fingal at 7.8 km. With both on, try 5 characters (8 found) and 6 (only Torcuil). Draw the quadtree at capacity 4: 40 boxes, Callander's 510 x 460 m, Catriona's 8.2 x 7.3 km. At capacity 1: 235.

explain.oneLine: Nobody hid Torcuil from the app. It searched one geohash cell, and a cell line ran between him and Catriona; the 7.8 km 'nearest' was only the nearest inside her box.

steps.title: Her position became a code, and the code is a box.
steps.text: A geohash turns a latitude and longitude into a short code. Halve the longitude range, -180 to 180, and write 1 if the point is in the eastern half or 0 if it's in the western; then halve the latitude range, -90 to 90, the same way, and keep alternating. That interleaves the longitude and latitude bits. Every 5 bits become one character in base 32, the digits and most of the letters. Catriona's 56.2512 N, 4.2885 W is gfhbn2. Every point whose code starts gfhb lies in one box, a cell, and each extra character splits the box into 32 smaller ones. Elasticsearch's table puts a 4-character cell at 39.1 km by 19.5 km at the equator. Cells narrow toward the poles, so at 56.25 N gfhb is 21.7 km wide along its southern edge and 19.5 km tall.

steps.title: A cell line can run between two people 400 m apart.
steps.text: Matching a prefix asks 'are you in my box?', not 'are you near me?'. Latitude 56.25 N is where the second character changes: just south it's gc, just north gf. Torcuil's hut, 400 m from Catriona, is gcuzyr; she is gfhbn2. They share only the first character, g, a cell about 5,000 km across. And two points in the same cell can be at opposite corners: gfhb is 29.2 km corner to corner. A shorter prefix doesn't help, because this line is a cell line at every length from 2 characters up. A longer one makes it worse, because a smaller cell puts more cell lines close to any point: at 5 and 6 characters her cell held nobody at all.

steps.title: The fix: nine cells, then real distance.
steps.text: Look up her cell and the 8 cells around it. Anyone closer to her than one cell's smaller side is then inside the nine, wherever the lines fall. Treat everyone found as a candidate, not an answer: work out each one's real distance with the haversine formula, sort, and page the nearest few. In the sim, the nine 4-character cells hold 27 available volunteers, and the nearest 3 are Torcuil at 400 m, Kilmahog at 2.6 km and Callander at 3.4 km. It takes both halves: the nine cells without ranking rang 27 phones, and ranking without the nine cells still paged Fingal at 7.8 km. Redis and many other systems work this way, a box search first and a distance check after.

steps.title: Pick the length from the search radius.
steps.text: The nine cells always reach at least one cell's smaller side past her: about 19.5 km at 4 characters, 2.7 km at 5 and 610 m at 6. So choose the longest prefix whose cells are still at least as big as the distance you need to search. To be sure of anyone within 15 km, use 4 characters. With 5, the nine cells found 8 volunteers tonight, enough this time but not promised; with 6, they found only Torcuil. If a search finds fewer people than you need, widen it: take the next ring of cells out, or drop a character, and rank again.

steps.title: Quadtrees: cells that fit the crowd.
steps.text: A fixed grid gives the empty hills and the middle of Callander the same size of cell, so a search in town reads a cell full of people and a search on the moor reads empty ones. A quadtree, described by Finkel and Bentley in 1974, starts with one box and splits it into four quarters whenever it holds more points than its leaf capacity, so boxes shrink where people crowd. In the sim, with a capacity of 4, the 60 phones make 40 leaves: Callander's is 510 x 460 m and Catriona's 8.2 x 7.3 km. Uber's H3 grid uses hexagons for the same job, and Google's S2 library cuts the sphere into cells.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn as nine 4-character cells. Top row, west to east: gfh9 with Tyndrum's volunteer, not available; gfhc with Killin; gfj1, nobody. Middle row: gfh8 with Crianlarich; gfhb, Catriona's cell, with Fingal at 7.8 km; gfj0 with St Fillans and Comrie. Bottom row: gcux, nobody; gcuz with Torcuil at 400 m, Kilmahog and west Callander; gcvp with east Callander, Doune and Dunblane. All nine feed a ranking step: 27 found, sorted by real distance, and the nearest 3 paged at 400 m, 2.6 km and 3.4 km.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next call. The app searches Catriona's cell, gfhb, and the eight around it, finds 27 available volunteers, works out each one's real distance and pages the nearest 3: Torcuil at 400 m in gcuz, Kilmahog at 2.6 km and Callander at 3.4 km.

fix.title: The fix: search nine cells, rank by real distance, page the nearest few
fix.text: Use the geohash only to fetch candidates. On a call, look up Catriona's 4-character cell and the eight cells around it, collect every available volunteer in the nine, work out each one's real distance with the haversine formula, sort, and page the nearest 3. Choose the prefix length from the distance the search must cover: with the eight cells added, 4 characters reaches at least 19.5 km from her in every direction here. If the nine cells hold fewer volunteers than you need, widen to the next ring. Where the nine cells hold far too many, as in a busy town, use smaller cells there, such as a quadtree's leaves.

limits: Nine cells only promise one cell's smaller side. If nobody is that close, someone just outside the nine can be nearer than anyone found, so widen the search before trusting the list.
Positions are only as fresh as each phone's last update. A volunteer who walked into a glen with no signal shows where they were, not where they are.
Haversine treats the Earth as a sphere and measures a straight line over it. Redis's docs put that error at up to 0.5%, and on a hill the walk can be far longer than the line.

explain.seniorTake: A spatial index answers 'who is in this box?', and a cell line can run anywhere, including between two people a few hundred metres apart. So use the index to fetch candidates and never to decide: search the cell and its neighbours, compute real distances, sort, and take the nearest few. Choose cell size from the radius you must cover, and from how crowded the area is: fixed grids are simple, and adaptive ones like quadtrees keep busy places cheap. Whatever the structure, the distance check at the end is what makes 'nearest' true.

realWorld.title: Geohash, 2008
realWorld.text: Wikipedia's article says geohash was invented in 2008 by Gustavo Niemeyer, who launched the website geohash.org. It warns of the weakness in this case: two points can be very close but have a short or no shared prefix. Its alphabet uses all digits 0-9 and all lower case letters except a, i, l and o.

realWorld.title: Elasticsearch: cell sizes by length
realWorld.text: Elasticsearch's geohash grid docs give cell sizes by geohash length and say the table is for the worst-case scenario at the equator: 3 characters 156.5km x 156km, 4 characters 39.1km x 19.5km, 5 characters 4.9km x 4.9km, 6 characters 1.2km x 609.4m. Cells narrow with latitude, which is why gfhb is 21.7 km wide.

realWorld.title: Redis GEOADD: a geohash score in a sorted set
realWorld.text: Redis's GEOADD docs say data is stored into the key as a sorted set, populated using a technique called Geohash: latitude and longitude bits are interleaved to form a unique 52-bit integer. They add that there is no GEODEL command, because the Geo index structure is just a sorted set.

realWorld.title: Redis: the 1+8 areas
realWorld.text: The same page says this format allows for bounding box and radius querying by checking the 1+8 areas needed to cover the whole shape and discarding elements outside it: the box and its eight neighbours, then a distance check. It assumes the Earth is a sphere and uses the Haversine formula, with an error of up to 0.5% in the worst case.

realWorld.title: Redis GEOSEARCH: nearest first
realWorld.text: GEOSEARCH searches within a circle (BYRADIUS) or an axis-aligned box (BYBOX), and ASC will sort the results by distance from the center: nearest first. COUNT returns at most that many matches; with ANY it returns as soon as enough matches are found, so the results may not be the ones closest to the specified point.

realWorld.title: PostGIS ST_DWithin
realWorld.text: PostGIS's ST_DWithin returns true if the geometries are within a given distance, in meters for geography. Its docs say the function call includes a bounding box comparison that makes use of any indexes that are available on the geometries: the same coarse box first, exact distance after.

realWorld.title: PostGIS: GiST and bounding boxes
realWorld.text: The PostGIS workshop says spatial indexes are unable to index the geometric features themselves and instead index the bounding boxes of the features, and that the USING GIST clause tells PostgreSQL to use the generic index structure (GIST) when building the index, an R-Tree in PostGIS.

realWorld.title: Uber H3, 2018
realWorld.text: Uber's engineering blog wrote: 'We decided to create H3 to combine the benefits of a hexagonal global grid system with a hierarchical indexing system.' Hexagons matter because a hexagon has only one distance between its centre point and its neighbours', compared to two distances for squares.

realWorld.title: Google S2
realWorld.text: The S2 library's site says it represents all data on a three-dimensional sphere and can approximate arbitrary regions as collections of discrete S2 cells.

realWorld.title: Finkel and Bentley, 1974
realWorld.text: R. A. Finkel and J. L. Bentley's paper 'Quad Trees: A Data Structure for Retrieval on Composite Keys', Acta Informatica volume 4, 1974, introduced the quadtree: each node splits its region into four, so points with two keys, such as latitude and longitude, can be searched by region.

asked: What is a geohash, and what is its weakness?
How would you store and query millions of moving points?
interview.answer: Store each driver's latest position in a geospatial index: Redis GEOADD, which keeps a 52-bit geohash as the score in a sorted set, or PostGIS with a GiST index and ST_DWithin. A geohash interleaves longitude and latitude bits and writes them in base 32; a prefix is a cell, and each extra character divides it into 32. Its weakness is the cell line: two points metres apart can have different prefixes, even from an early character, and two in one cell can be its width apart. So never treat 'same prefix' as 'near'. For a query, take the rider's cell and its 8 neighbours at a length whose cell side covers the search radius, compute the real distance to every candidate, sort, and return the nearest k; GEOSEARCH with BYRADIUS, ASC and COUNT does this for you. Widen the ring if you find too few. For millions of moving points, overwrite each driver's position on every update so you keep one entry per driver, drop drivers who go offline, and shard by region. In dense cities fixed cells hold too many drivers, so use smaller cells there: a quadtree, or H3 or S2 at a finer resolution.

terms.def: Volunteers who search for and help people lost or hurt in the hills, called out by phone, day or night. The Corrieburn team has 60.
Asking volunteers to turn out for a rescue. The Corrieburn desk takes the call and the app pages volunteers.
To send an urgent alert that makes someone's phone ring or buzz until they answer. Paging the whole team rings every phone.
A yes or no a volunteer sets in the app to say they can turn out right now. The app only pages volunteers whose flag is on, unless it pages the whole team.
How far north or south of the equator a point is, in degrees from -90 to 90. Ben Ledi's ridge is at about 56.25 N.
How far east or west of the line through Greenwich a point is, in degrees from -180 to 180. Ben Ledi is at about 4.29 W, that is -4.29.
A short code for a place: halve the longitude range, then the latitude range, again and again, record each half as a bit, and write the bits in base 32. 56.2512 N, 4.2885 W is gfhbn2.
To take bits from two sources in turn. A geohash takes one bit of longitude, then one of latitude, then longitude again, and so on.
Writing numbers with 32 symbols, so each symbol holds 5 bits. Geohash uses the digits 0 to 9 and the lower-case letters except a, i, l and o.
The first few characters of a geohash. Every point whose code starts with the same prefix lies in the same cell; gfhb is the 4-character prefix of gfhbn2.
The box of the map that one geohash prefix stands for. Each extra character splits it into 32. At 56.25 N a 4-character cell is 21.7 km wide and 19.5 km tall.
The edge between two cells. Points a few metres apart on either side of it get different prefixes. On Ben Ledi one runs along 56.25 N.
The 8 cells that touch a cell at its sides and corners. A search of a cell and its 8 neighbours covers 9 cells in all.
A formula for the distance between two points along the surface of a sphere, from their latitudes and longitudes. The sim uses a sphere of radius 6371 km.
Sorting the volunteers found by their real distance from the caller, nearest first, so the app can page the nearest few.
How far from the caller a search must be sure to look. It sets the prefix length: the cells must be at least that big.
A volunteer the cell search found who might be among the nearest. Each one's real distance is then checked before anyone is paged.
A tree of boxes: each box splits into four quarters when it holds more points than its leaf capacity. Crowded places end up with small boxes and empty ones with big boxes.
A box in a quadtree that has not been split. Its points are stored in it directly. With capacity 4, the team's 60 phones make 40 leaves.
The most points a quadtree leaf may hold before it splits into four. A smaller capacity gives more, smaller leaves.
An index built for positions or shapes on a map, also called a geospatial index, so a database can find what lies in or near an area without reading every row.
A Redis data type that keeps unique members, each with a number called its score, in order of score, so a range of scores is fast to read.
The number Redis sorts a sorted set's members by. GEOADD stores each place's 52-bit geohash as its score.
The Redis command that adds places (longitude, latitude, name) to a key, stored as a sorted set with each place's geohash as its score.
The Redis command that finds the places within a circle (BYRADIUS) or box (BYBOX) around a point. ASC sorts them nearest first and COUNT limits how many come back.
The smallest upright rectangle that contains a shape or an area. Spatial indexes compare boxes first because it is cheap, and check exact shapes or distances after.
An extension that adds map shapes, distances and spatial indexes to PostgreSQL.
A PostGIS function that is true when two shapes are within a given distance. It compares bounding boxes using any index first.
Generalized Search Tree: PostgreSQL's framework for index types beyond the B-tree. PostGIS uses it to build R-tree spatial indexes.
A tree index of bounding boxes, each parent box enclosing its children's. A search walks only the boxes that overlap the area asked for.
Uber's open-source grid that covers the Earth in hexagons at many sizes, with each hexagon's neighbours all the same distance from its centre.
Google's open-source geometry library. It works on a sphere and divides it into cells at many levels.
A GDPR principle, Article 5(1)(c): personal data should be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for its purpose.
A GDPR principle, Article 5(1)(e): personal data should be kept in a form that identifies people for no longer than necessary for its purpose.

atWork: Look for anything in your systems that finds 'things near a point': couriers, drivers, stores, technicians, delivery slots. A common incident runs like this: a delivery app shows 'couriers near you' by matching the customer's geohash prefix, and support tickets pile up from customers who waited twenty minutes while a courier idled across the street, in the next cell. Check three things. Does the search look at the neighbouring cells, or only the customer's own? Does it compute a real distance to each candidate and sort, or does a matching prefix count as 'near'? And is the prefix length chosen from the radius the product promises? If you use Redis, GEOSEARCH with BYRADIUS, ASC and COUNT does the neighbour search and the sort for you; in PostgreSQL, ST_DWithin with a GiST index. Then look at what you store. A worker's live position is personal data. If your company is subject to the GDPR, its data minimisation principle (Article 5(1)(c)) and storage limitation principle (Article 5(1)(e)) point to keeping only the latest position, only while the person is available or on shift, and deleting it when they go off; a history of every position you never use is the kind of thing an assessor can ask about, so decide it in the design rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your delivery app shows 'couriers near you' by listing couriers whose 6-character geohash matches the customer's. Support says customers sometimes wait twenty minutes while the map shows a courier across the street, and other times the app finds no courier at all in a busy area. What is going wrong, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The customer and the courier are in different cells: a cell boundary runs between them, so a prefix match misses close points
Search the customer's cell and its 8 neighbouring cells, not just one
Compute the real distance to every candidate, sort, and show the nearest few

recall.model: A prefix match only says two points share a cell, and a cell boundary can run between a customer and a courier across the street, so the courier is in a different cell and never listed. A 6-character cell is small, so cell lines are close to everyone, and sometimes the customer's own cell holds nobody. Search the customer's cell and its 8 neighbouring cells instead, choosing a prefix length whose cells are at least as big as the radius you promise, then compute the real distance to every courier found, sort nearest first and show the nearest few. If nine cells hold too few, widen to the next ring.

recall.prompt: What does adding one more character to a geohash prefix do to its cell?
options: Halves the cell along its longer side
Divides the cell into 32 smaller cells
Divides the cell into 4 smaller cells
Moves the cell to the next one east
recall.why: Each base 32 character carries 5 bits, alternating longitude and latitude, so one more character splits the cell into 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32 smaller ones. That's why a 4-character cell at 56.25 N is 21.7 km by 19.5 km and a 5-character cell only 2.7 km by 4.9 km. Splitting into 4 is what one quadtree step does.

recall.prompt: Design the backend for 'find drivers near me' in a city with 50,000 drivers, each sending a position every 4 seconds. A rider opens the app and wants the 10 closest drivers within 3 km. How would you store the positions and answer the query?

keyIdeas.idea: Keep positions in a geospatial index, such as Redis GEOADD (geohash scores in a sorted set) or PostGIS with a GiST index
Search the area around the rider including neighbouring cells, then compute real distances, sort, and take the closest 10
Overwrite each driver's latest position on every update and drop drivers who go offline, so data stays small and fresh

recall.model: Keep each driver's position in a geospatial index: Redis GEOADD, which stores a 52-bit geohash as the score in a sorted set, is a good fit at 50,000 drivers, or PostGIS with a GiST index. Each update overwrites the driver's latest position, so there is one entry per driver, and drivers who go offline are removed. For the query, use GEOSEARCH with BYRADIUS 3 km, ASC and COUNT 10: it reads the rider's cell and its neighbours, computes the real distance to each candidate, sorts nearest first and returns the closest 10. In dense areas, smaller cells keep the candidate list short.

recall.prompt: Catriona was at 56.2512 N, 4.2885 W and Torcuil's hut at 56.2477 N, 4.2870 W, 400 m apart. How many characters of their geohashes match?
recall.why: She is gfhbn2 and the hut is gcuzyr. 56.25 N is where the second character changes, gc to the south and gf to the north, so they share only the g, a cell about 5,000 km across. Being close never promises a long shared prefix.

recall.prompt: Redis's GEOSEARCH can take COUNT with the ANY option. According to the Redis docs, what does ANY give up?
options: That the coordinates are stored exactly
That the results are the ones closest to the point
That the results lie inside the shape searched
That each place is stored only once
recall.why: The docs say that with ANY the command returns as soon as enough matches are found, which is faster, but the results may be unsorted and may not be the ones closest to the specified point. Without ANY it finds every match in the area and sorts them, which costs more on a large area.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The nine cells and the ranking work; Torcuil has been paged first twice this summer. In August the regional association put every team on our app: 1,400 volunteers, about 900 of them in and around Stirling and Perth. Now a call from just outside Stirling makes the nine 4-character cells return over a thousand volunteers, and the app works out a distance to every one of them before it pages anyone, which takes long enough on the old desk laptop that we've started paging by hand. And on Rannoch Moor, last week, the nine cells held one volunteer, 18 km away, and the developer isn't sure he was the nearest.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does one fixed cell size fail in both places, and what should the app do instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Use cells that fit the density: a quadtree, or finer cells where people crowd and coarser where they don't
Start with a small area and widen ring by ring until enough candidates are found, so no one nearer is left outside
Still rank the candidates by real distance and page only the nearest few

coldCase.model: A 4-character cell is about 20 km across whatever is in it, so near Stirling nine of them hold over a thousand people and on Rannoch Moor they hold one. Use cells that fit the density instead: a quadtree splits a box whenever it holds more than its leaf capacity, so towns get small cells and the moor big ones, or use finer geohash cells where it's crowded. Then search outward: start with the caller's small cell and its neighbours and widen ring by ring until you have enough candidates and the nearest one found is closer than the edge of the area searched; on the moor that means widening past 18 km before trusting him. Finally rank the candidates by real distance and page the nearest few, so the desk only ever sorts a handful.
